item.title: Newborn Kitten Found Covered in Ants Was Denied Help Door After Door, Now Follows His New Friend Everywhere
item.description:
Three teenagers found a newborn kitten alone on the streets of California, covered in red ants. Door after door, they were denied help until someone finally said yes. Now the kitten follows his new friend everywhere.

JinxCredit: Merced SPCA

That kitten is Jinx, and he was only a few days old when he was found, his eyes barely open and his body far too small to be on his own.

The teenagers who found him had already tried everywhere they could think of in Merced and neighboring Atwater, and kept being told no. Still, they would not give up on him.

They went block by block, neighborhood by neighborhood, knocking on door after door, looking for anyone who would help. Before they set out, they had tucked him into a box, wrapped him in a soft blanket, and made sure he had a little to eat.

The day he was found, small enough to fit in one handCredit: Merced SPCA

Jinx was so small he fit in the palm of one hand, a scrap of gray fur that could have been missed by anyone not looking closely. The teenagers who found him were not willing to look away.

Most people would have kept walking past a kitten that tiny and that fragile. These three decided his life was worth knocking on every door in town.

Carried door to door in a box until someone could helpCredit: Merced SPCA

With Jinx bundled in his box, they carried him from house to house, refusing to stop until they found someone who could take him in. The knocking is what kept him going, one more door at a time.

That persistence finally paid off in a way none of them could have planned.

Safe at last, tucked into a warm blanket.Credit: Merced SPCA

By chance, they ended up at the home of Cynthia Kelly, who leads Merced SPCA, an all-volunteer, foster-based, no-kill rescue. At that very moment, the group’s secretary, Lyric Adam, was pulling into the driveway to pick up food and vaccines.

Lyric, who fosters the rescue’s bottle and neonatal babies, got out, listened to the teenagers’ story, and took Jinx into her care on the spot. She cleaned the ants from his fur, warmed him up, and looked him over before settling in for the round-the-clock care a kitten his age needs.

“I’m not even sure if they got to knock before I pulled up,” Lyric shared with LoveMeow. After all those doors, the one that finally opened came down to pure timing, the kind that only found him because three kids kept knocking.

Calm after milk meowsCredit: Merced SPCA

Jinx was very skinny, and his eyes were only just beginning to open, the first hints of blue starting to peek through. His ears were still closed, folded flat the way they are in the earliest days of life.

Little by little, the signs of a thriving kitten began to show. His eyes opened wider every day, and he found his voice, letting out tiny meows that said he was not going anywhere.

Feeding timeCredit: Merced SPCA

Lyric fed him with a Miracle Nipple, a feeding syringe made for the tiniest babies, and Jinx took to it with enthusiasm, latching on hungrily at every meal. A little stuffed animal was tucked in beside him so he would not have to feel so alone.

For a baby who started life without his mother, that soft companion made his small world feel a little less empty. And as it turned out, Jinx would not be the only little one in the house for long.

Vi, who arrived not long after JinxCredit: Merced SPCA

Not long after, another tiny face made her way to Merced SPCA. Vi was found dumped outside, tucked under a tree and trying to keep herself warm.

She got a good meal and a safe place to rest, and after a short stint of what the rescue fondly called “office desk life,” she headed to the same foster home, where a familiar little face was waiting.

From the first day, Jinx wanted to be wherever Vi wasCredit: Merced SPCA

From the moment they were under the same roof, Jinx became completely taken with his new friend. He watches everything Vi does as though she is the most interesting thing in the world, following wherever she goes and studying whatever she is up to.

Vi seems just as glad to have him there, keeping an eye on Jinx and whatever small adventure he is about to get into next.

Two little rescues, growing up as a pairCredit: Merced SPCA

Vi still has weight to gain and is working her way back on a special diet and medication, taking foster life one day at a time with Jinx right beside her.

Two kittens who each started alone, one covered in ants and one left under a tree, found their way to the same warm room and to each other. Neither of them has to face the rest of it on their own again.

Share this story with your friends. View more on Jinx, Vi, and the Merced SPCA team on Instagram @mercedspca and Facebook.

item.title: We Asked Five Cat Rescues in Five States If They Were Full. All Five Named a Cause No One Expected
item.description:
LoveMeow asked five cat rescues in five states one question this week: are you at or over capacity? One has paused intake since summer, another has taken in more cats than in any year of its history, and all five pointed at the same thing.

Clio and CalypsoCredit: Little Wanderers NYC

The rescues were Abandoned Pet Rescue in Fort Lauderdale, Florida; Little Wanderers NYC; Whiskers-A-GoGo in Brooklyn; Sparkle Cat Rescue in Burlington, North Carolina; and Homeward Bound Cat Adoptions in Las Vegas. Four of the five operate entirely through foster homes with no shelter building. One has paused intake since summer. One has taken in more cats in ten months than in any full year of its history.

Their answers describe something more specific than full shelters, and more fixable.

Every rescue named the same cause

LoveMeow did not ask any of these organizations about spay and neuter programs. All five raised it on their own.

AnaCredit: Sparkle Cat Rescue

Kara Starzyk, executive director of Abandoned Pet Rescue, named it as the single biggest factor alongside a shortage of trap-neuter-return programs. In her state, the consequence is structural: Florida's climate lets cats breed year-round, so there is no winter pause to let a shelter population fall.

"Our shelter has long been at capacity, it's a revolving door," Starzyk told J. Allen of LoveMeow. "Because we are a private shelter, we can only take in pets when we have space available. When one goes out, a waitlist plus others are trying to come in constantly." Her organization fields around 30 calls, emails, and walk-ins a day, roughly half of them for cats.

Stephanie Grantham, president of Sparkle Cat Rescue, said people in her area are struggling to find affordable spay and neuter services, and that the shortage feeds directly back into intake. The result, she told LoveMeow, is that "the cycle just goes on and on."

In New York City, Lisa Scroggins of Little Wanderers NYC framed it as a funding question. "If there was city help and funding for spay/neuter services and rescue requests, we'd really be attacking the root of the problem," she told Megan Marie of LoveMeow.

The pattern is not limited to the organizations LoveMeow contacted. In Jim Thorpe, Pennsylvania, Carbon County Friends of Animals stopped accepting cats entirely in October after running out of cages. President Susie Yaich told the Times News that low-cost spay and neuter appointments in her area were booked until late November.

"It's not necessarily a no. Often, it's a not right now."

Homeward Bound Cat Adoptions admitted 1,736 cats in the first ten months of 2026, more than in any full year since it began keeping these records. Its admissions are also booked several weeks out.

Freeway Credit: Homeward Bound Cats

Both things are true at once, and that is the part the simple version of this story misses.

"Capacity for care is about so much more than having a space," said Kimberly Wade, consultant for marketing and operations at Homeward Bound. "It's having enough people, time, funding, medical resources, and space to meet every animal's physical and emotional needs. We have to be able to properly care for the cats already counting on us before we can responsibly take in more."

Asked directly whether the rescue was turning cats away, Wade declined the premise. "We're not necessarily saying no. Often, it's a 'not right now,'" she told LoveMeow. "Our admissions are booked several weeks out, so we evaluate each situation individually, prioritize urgent cases, and work with people to find the best available option for their cats."

The organization's admissions over five years show what absorbing a rising caseload looks like from inside.

YearCats admitted% Change
2022849
20231,007+18.6%
2024952-5.5%
20251,688+77.3%
2026, thru October1,736+2.8%

That is 104.5% growth in four years, with November and December still to come.

"Under new leadership, over the past three years we've made a lot of intentional changes to our programs, operations, and use of resources, and those changes have allowed us to help more cats than Homeward Bound has ever been able to before," executive director Vanessa Porter said in a statement to LoveMeow. "While we're extremely proud of that, the real story isn't the numbers. It's that hundreds more cats are receiving the care, medical treatment, and second chances they deserve."

Porter was direct about the trend underneath her own growth. "More people are reaching out for help, more cats are entering the system, and animal welfare organizations across the country are facing increasing pressure," she said. "This isn't a challenge unique to Homeward Bound."

For most rescues, capacity is people

Four of the five organizations have no building. Their ceiling is a headcount of volunteers and a bank balance.

Twix and Kit Kat Credit: Abandoned Pet Rescue

Sparkle Cat Rescue has paused intake since the summer, and Grantham laid out the sequence in one breath. "Our intake this year has been way down because adoptions are slow. Donations have been down both monetarily and supply-wise. People are not applying to foster when we ask, and we simply cannot help cats when those three things occur."

The effect compounds. "Kittens are growing up in foster care and adult cats have not found homes," she said.

Eva Prokop of Whiskers-A-GoGo described the same arithmetic. "We are a foster-based rescue, not an open intake shelter, so we never intake all cats and kittens we are offered or asked to intake," she told J. Allen of LoveMeow. "Our capacity depends on our fosters and financial situation." Her rescue's response is to grow the network rather than ration it: "We try to increase our capacity by growing our foster network, training and inspiring them."

Prokop was also clear that her situation is not the hardest one. "We think that open intake shelters, municipal shelters contracted by municipalities as animal control, are in a much more difficult situation." Those shelters are obligated to accept every animal brought to them.

Scroggins made the case that foster networks reach places a building cannot. Little Wanderers works in some of the hardest-hit areas of New York City and provides direct services in low-income communities, and its volume, she said, rivals that of brick-and-mortar shelters. "Nonprofit grassroots groups like Little Wanderers are crushed by endless requests," she said. "Our volunteer team is remarkable."

New York's foster networks are also working under new rules. The state's Companion Animal Care Standards Act took effect on December 15, 2025, and includes a personnel training section. According to Prokop, fosters must now complete a training course before taking animals in, on top of each rescue's own requirements. "We make sure to match fosters with animals that they are comfortable caring for, age, socialization, etc.," she said.

Then 26 cats arrived from one house

Last week Homeward Bound agreed to take a group of 26 cats and kittens from a single family, arranging the intake in stages so its medical team could keep up. Then the family told them there were another 12 kittens and two mother cats who had to be out within two days.

Multiple litters in 1 day Credit: Homeward Bound Cats

The family had contacted other organizations without getting a response. They had no money to pay for help. The kittens needed urgent veterinary attention, and without somewhere to go, they would be left outside to fend for themselves.

Homeward Bound was already past the capacity it considers responsible.

"When we know we're someone's only option, we do everything we can to find a way to help," Wade said. "We never want to see cats and kittens suffer or be abandoned simply because the system is overwhelmed. Sometimes that means getting creative and figuring out how to make room when we thought we had none."

They took all 40.

What the people doing this work say helps

Every organization pointed at the same two levers, in the same order.

Eliza Hamilton Credit: Little Wanderers NYC

Adoption, because it is the only thing that creates room. "Every adoption does more than change one cat's life," Wade said. "It creates space, frees up resources, and allows us to say yes to another cat who needs help." Homeward Bound has more than 80 cats and kittens waiting. Starzyk put it the same way: "When you adopt, you are not only helping one animal find a home, you're helping other animals come into a safe space."

And affordable spay and neuter, because it is the only thing that reduces the number of cats needing rescue at all. Four of the five named it as the root cause, and none described it as solved anywhere.

Starzyk raised one more pattern her shelter sees often, and it is preventable. Older cat owners frequently have no plan for their animals. When something happens to the owner medically, and no arrangement exists, the cat ends up at a shelter.

What one open slot looks like

The numbers in this story are large enough to blur. It is worth remembering what a single opening in a foster network actually produces.

Truly Scrumptious Credit: Whiskers-A-GoGo

Whiskers-A-GoGo adopted out a gray kitten named Truly Scrumptious in 2022. Years later, after his adopter's relationship ended, he was passed between homes until he ended up on a Brooklyn sidewalk. A rescuer found him there and did the one thing that changed everything: she scanned him. The microchip led straight back to Whiskers-A-GoGo, which had never stopped being listed as his people.

They had room. It took him about three weeks to understand the moving had stopped. What emerged was a cat who holds hands while he is being cuddled and plays fetch with toy mice.

Every rescue in this story is deciding, several times a day, how many of those they can say yes to.

How to help

This week is National Animal Shelter Appreciation Week, which the people in this story will spend at or beyond their capacity for care. Every organization named here takes adoptions, foster applications, donations, and volunteers.

  • Abandoned Pet Rescue, Fort Lauderdale, Florida
  • Little Wanderers NYC, New York City
  • Sparkle Cat Rescue, Burlington, North Carolina
  • Whiskers-A-GoGo, Brooklyn, New York
  • Homeward Bound Cat Adoptions, Las Vegas, Nevada

LoveMeow has reported on cats from three of these organizations before, including a cat family left in a bird cage outside Abandoned Pet Rescue, Truly Scrumptious and the microchip that brought him back to Whiskers-A-GoGo, and a kitten pulled off a Las Vegas freeway exit ramp by Homeward Bound.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are animal shelters full of cats right now?


Many are at or beyond what they describe as a comfortable capacity for care. A shelter in Jim Thorpe, Pennsylvania stopped accepting cats entirely in October after running out of cages. Several foster-based rescues told LoveMeow their admissions are booked weeks out or paused. But capacity is not only about space: four of the five organizations LoveMeow spoke to have no shelter building at all, and their limit is the number of available foster homes and the funding to cover veterinary care.

Why are so many cats entering shelters?


Every rescue LoveMeow spoke to named the same primary cause: a shortage of accessible low-cost spay and neuter services, and in some areas a shortage of trap-neuter-return programs. In warm-climate states such as Florida, cats breed year-round, so there is no seasonal pause. Rescues also reported adoptions and donations falling, which slows the rate at which cats leave and reduces the resources available to take in more.

What is the difference between an open-intake shelter and a foster-based rescue?


An open-intake shelter, usually a municipal facility contracted as animal control, is obligated to accept animals brought to it. A limited-admission or foster-based rescue can decide what it is able to take on responsibly, which is why its admissions may be scheduled weeks in advance. Several rescues noted that open-intake shelters face the harder version of this problem because they cannot decline.

What actually helps a shelter that is over capacity?


Adoption, because it is the only thing that frees space and resources. Fostering, because for most rescues the number of foster homes is the real ceiling rather than the number of cages. Donations, because veterinary care is the largest cost a rescue carries. And wider access to affordable spay and neuter, which is what every organization in this story named as the root cause.

How can I help cat shelters?


Six things, drawn from what the rescues in this story said they need most.

  • Adopt an adult cat. Kittens move quickly. Sparkle Cat Rescue reported the opposite problem, that "adult cats have not found homes" while kittens grew up in foster care waiting.
  • Say yes to a bonded pair. Pairs wait considerably longer than single cats because fewer adopters will take two, even though bonded cats are often easier to settle because they already have each other.
  • Foster, even briefly. For a foster-based rescue, one additional foster home is one additional cat it can say yes to. Whiskers-A-GoGo matches fosters to animals they are comfortable caring for, so a first-time foster is not handed the hardest case.
  • Donate supplies as well as money. Sparkle Cat Rescue reported donations down "both monetarily and supply wise." Most rescues publish a wish list.
  • Spay or neuter your own cat, and help a neighbor do the same. This is the root cause every organization named. If cost is the barrier, ask local rescues which low-cost clinics they use.
  • Make a plan for your cat. Kara Starzyk of Abandoned Pet Rescue said one pattern her shelter sees repeatedly is older owners with no arrangement in place. When something happens to the owner medically and nobody has agreed to take the cat, the cat arrives at a shelter. Naming someone willing to take your animal, in writing, prevents that.

Advocacy is the seventh. Little Wanderers NYC asked specifically for city funding for spay and neuter services, which is a decision made by local government rather than by rescues.

  • Little Wanderers NYC, New York City
  • Sparkle Cat Rescue, Burlington, North Carolina
  • Whiskers-A-GoGo, Brooklyn, New York
  • Homeward Bound Cat Adoptions, Las Vegas, Nevada

LoveMeow has reported on cats from three of these organizations before, including a cat family left in a bird cage outside Abandoned Pet Rescue, Truly Scrumptious and the microchip that brought him back to Whiskers-A-GoGo, and a kitten pulled off a Las Vegas freeway exit ramp by Homeward Bound.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are animal shelters full of cats right now?


Many are at or beyond what they describe as a comfortable capacity for care. A shelter in Jim Thorpe, Pennsylvania stopped accepting cats entirely in October after running out of cages. Several foster-based rescues told LoveMeow their admissions are booked weeks out or paused. But capacity is not only about space: four of the five organizations LoveMeow spoke to have no shelter building at all, and their limit is the number of available foster homes and the funding to cover veterinary care.

Why are so many cats entering shelters?


Every rescue LoveMeow spoke to named the same primary cause: a shortage of accessible low-cost spay and neuter services, and in some areas a shortage of trap-neuter-return programs. In warm-climate states such as Florida, cats breed year-round, so there is no seasonal pause. Rescues also reported adoptions and donations falling, which slows the rate at which cats leave and reduces the resources available to take in more.

What is the difference between an open-intake shelter and a foster-based rescue?


An open-intake shelter, usually a municipal facility contracted as animal control, is obligated to accept animals brought to it. A limited-admission or foster-based rescue can decide what it is able to take on responsibly, which is why its admissions may be scheduled weeks in advance. Several rescues noted that open-intake shelters face the harder version of this problem because they cannot decline.

What actually helps a shelter that is over capacity?


Adoption, because it is the only thing that frees space and resources. Fostering, because for most rescues the number of foster homes is the real ceiling rather than the number of cages. Donations, because veterinary care is the largest cost a rescue carries. And wider access to affordable spay and neuter, which is what every organization in this story named as the root cause.

How can I help cat shelters?


Six things, drawn from what the rescues in this story said they need most.

  • Adopt an adult cat. Kittens move quickly. Sparkle Cat Rescue reported the opposite problem, that "adult cats have not found homes" while kittens grew up in foster care waiting.
  • Say yes to a bonded pair. Pairs wait considerably longer than single cats because fewer adopters will take two, even though bonded cats are often easier to settle because they already have each other.
  • Foster, even briefly. For a foster-based rescue, one additional foster home is one additional cat it can say yes to. Whiskers-A-GoGo matches fosters to animals they are comfortable caring for, so a first-time foster is not handed the hardest case.
  • Donate supplies as well as money. Sparkle Cat Rescue reported donations down "both monetarily and supply wise." Most rescues publish a wish list.
  • Spay or neuter your own cat, and help a neighbor do the same. This is the root cause every organization named. If cost is the barrier, ask local rescues which low-cost clinics they use.
  • Make a plan for your cat. Kara Starzyk of Abandoned Pet Rescue said one pattern her shelter sees repeatedly is older owners with no arrangement in place. When something happens to the owner medically and nobody has agreed to take the cat, the cat arrives at a shelter. Naming someone willing to take your animal, in writing, prevents that.

Advocacy is the seventh. Little Wanderers NYC asked specifically for city funding for spay and neuter services, which is a decision made by local government rather than by rescues.

item.title: Kitten Found Injured and Covered in Paint at Construction Site Healed With His Sister’s Comfort Along The Way
item.description:
A black kitten was found covered in paint at a construction site, badly hurt and barely holding on, and the thing that seemed to keep the little black kitten going was his orange sister, found with him.

VinnyCredit: Leo’s Friends Rescue

Vinny, short for Vincent and named for the paint that nearly killed him, is a healthy, bright-eyed kitten today. A year ago, almost no one thought he would live to see it.

The call came from a construction site, where crews demolishing a building found a tiny kitten smothered in paint. Struck by a paint can, he had a broken leg and a head injury, and he was fading fast.

Safe to play again Credit: Leo’s Friends Rescue

He was not alone. A small orange sister, Vivienne, was curled right beside him, untouched, already doing the thing she would keep doing for weeks to come: keeping her brother warm.

The day they were foundCredit: Leo’s Friends Rescue

Lindsay, a medical foster with Leo’s Friends Rescue, did not hesitate. She drove out to collect the pair and get them to safety, even in the middle of an already hard day.

Faced with a decision about where Vinny had the best chance, she followed her gut and drove the long way to her trusted vet. “I couldn’t give up control over his fate,” Lindsay shared with LoveMeow.

Cleaned, shaved, and bandaged, with a long road aheadCredit: Leo’s Friends Rescue

The drive was harrowing. Vinny kept crashing, and Lindsay dripped apple juice into his mouth the whole way, praying he would hold on. One drop at a time, mile after mile, it was the only thing she could do to keep him with her.

At the clinic, he was cleaned, then shaved, and given fluids. With a broken leg and how little he was responding, the team feared a serious head injury, and no one could say whether he would pull through.

Signs of a fighterCredit: Leo’s Friends Rescue

Lindsay decided to give him time, and took both kittens home to foster. Just a few hours after they arrived, Vinny did something that brought her to tears. He started meowing again.

Through those first fragile days, Vivienne barely moved from his side. She snuggled close and kept him warm, her small body and steady heartbeat comforting him at his worst.

Healing togetherCredit: Leo’s Friends Rescue

The rescue is convinced Vivienne is part of why her brother lived. “We truly believe having Vivi by his side played a huge part in his recovery,” Lindsay shared, crediting the warm snuggles and comforting heartbeat that kept him going.

Lindsay trusted what she saw in him, too. “If there’s a glimmer behind those eyes, listen to them,” she shared, and Vinny, it turned out, had plenty of glimmer left.

Cast and all, with Vivienne making her pointCredit: Leo’s Friends Rescue

He surprised everyone. A little better one day, stronger the next, and before long he was walking again, cast and all, keeping pace with his sister step for step.

Vivienne kept pace with opinions of her own, one paw often raised as though she had something to add to the conversation. Whatever Vinny was doing, she was right in the middle of it.

Knows the best camera anglesCredit: Leo’s Friends Rescue

The feared head injury never showed itself. The cast came off, his eyesight was perfectly fine, and the kitten who had so nearly slipped away was declared completely healthy. “An absolute miracle,” Lindsay shared. “We genuinely didn’t know if he would pull through, but he did.”

Today Vinny is a sleek, bright-eyed charmer with no sign of the state he arrived in. The paint, the cast, the terrifying drive are all behind him.

Happily be carried everywhereCredit: Leo’s Friends Rescue

Vivienne came through it all untouched and grew into the gentlest, most affectionate girl imaginable. “She loves to lay in your lap and get cuddles and be held like a baby,” Lindsay shared, and she melts into the arms of anyone who will hold her.

Her devotion to her brother never faded. The two have never spent a day apart, and if they are separated even briefly, they cry out for each other until they are back together.

Vivi growing upCredit: Leo’s Friends Rescue

These days the pair nap with their arms wrapped around each other, Vivienne’s face nestled into her brother’s soft fur. Wherever one of them goes, the other follows.

Vinny was found covered in paint and barely breathing, with Vivienne pressed close beside him. Today, the two of them are whole, wonderful, and every bit the cats Lindsay bet on.

Vinny & VivienneCredit: Leo’s Friends Rescue

Vinny and Vivienne are looking for a home together, because after everything, these two are not meant to be apart.

item.title: Four Kittens Beside a Canal Stayed Huddled Together Through the Night and Now Dive Into Dinner All at Once
item.description:
Four kittens left alone beside a canal stayed huddled through the night, together, until a couple who stumbled upon them refused to give up on them. Now they dive into their dinner plates all at once.

Baccarat, Cribbage, Euchre, and RummyCredit: The Stray Cat Club

The four were found in an unlikely place, perched right at the edge of a canal, a long way from the nearest path, with no mother cat to be found.

It had the look of a dumping. The Stray Cat Club, a London rescue that sees more dumped litters than it would like, would eventually take them in. “Dumped kittens honestly break us, and sadly, we suspect this may be another case,” the rescue shared with LoveMeow.

Most people would have kept walking. A special couple did the opposite and decided these kittens needed a better outcome.

Exactly where they were found, huddled in the brush by the waterCredit: The Stray Cat Club

Worried for the kittens, the couple bought them food and settled in to wait, hoping their mother might come back. She never did.

As darkness came on, they could not bring themselves to leave the babies exposed. They sought advice and built a small shelter right where the kittens sat, determined to get them through the night.

Safe in a carrier at lastCredit: The Stray Cat Club

They barely slept. Early the next morning, they hurried back, bracing for the worst, and found all four kittens still there, snuggled together in a pile exactly where they had left them. After a night of worrying, the relief of seeing four little faces still warm and breathing was its own reward.

They fed the hungry babies and came back again that afternoon. By then it was clear the kittens were on their own and would not last out there, so the couple made sure all four were brought safely into the rescue’s care.

One of the three black siblingsCredit: The Stray Cat Club

The rescue is still a little awed by what the finders did. “We can’t thank their finders enough for making that journey again and again, watching over them and making sure they weren’t left behind,” the rescue shared with LoveMeow.

It was no short trip, either. The canal spot was a twenty-minute walk from the nearest access point, and the couple made that walk back and forth, morning and evening, all weekend long. Their persistence is the entire reason these four are here.

The lone tortoiseshell of the bunchCredit: The Stray Cat Club

Once they were in care, the kittens turned out to be surprisingly solid little things. “They’re surprisingly chunky little things, although we’re yet to discover whether those round bellies are full of food or worms,” the rescue shared at first. The answer, happily, was food. A full check came back clean across the board, litter trained, eating well, clean coats, bright eyes, and no health concerns at all, and they have put on even more weight in the days since.

The four came away with a theme for names. Baccarat, Cribbage, Euchre, and Rummy are all named for card games, a fitting set for four siblings who are never found apart. Three of them are black, which makes the one tortoiseshell an easy one to pick out of the pile.

Four faces down. Dinner is serious businessCredit: The Stray Cat Club

They have taken to mealtimes with real enthusiasm. Line up the bowls and all four dive in at once, a row of little tails tucked in and not a sound but contented eating.

For babies who spent a weekend waiting on food a stranger had to carry in, a full bowl on demand is a luxury they do not take for granted.

Bright-eyed and completely unbothered by companyCredit: The Stray Cat Club

The biggest surprise is how sociable they are. “They’re also incredibly friendly, which makes us wonder even more about how they ended up there,” the rescue said.

Healthy, well-fed, and sweet-natured, with not a single concern among them, the four carry every sign of having been cared for once. The clean bill of health and the easy, trusting nature make the rescue certain these kittens were dumped rather than born wild.

One of four, safe and soundCredit: The Stray Cat Club

In care, the four do everything as a unit, tumbling into the same bed and lining up at the same bowls, just as they were when the couple found them.

Their story could so easily have ended beside that canal. Instead, Baccarat, Cribbage, Euchre, and Rummy are warm, fed, and piled together, and for the first time in their short lives, they get to do all their growing somewhere safe.

Ready for next adventure Credit: The Stray Cat Club

Share this story with your friends. More on Baccarat, Cribbage, Euchre, Rummy, and The Stray Cat Club on [Instagram @thestraycatclub and Facebook.

item.title: Stray Cat Settled Into a Foster Room, Then Had Five Kittens Overnight, Already Cleaned and Nursing by Morning
item.description:
A stray cat, pregnant out on the streets with no one to help her arrived into the care of a Foster with a cozy room to give birth. She had her five kittens overnight and they were all cleaned and nursing by morning.

AbbyCredit: Snuggle Fluff

Abby came to the Pet Alliance, a shelter based in Central Florida, as a friendly stray, pregnant and nearly ready to give birth. She was taken by a calm foster with a room to settle in, and she wasted no time making herself at home.

After a relaxing few days, she decided it was time. Her foster woke up one morning to a surprise, five healthy kittens already cleaned, dried, and nursing, every one of them latched on.

This was not Abby’s first litter. She had raised kittens before, out on the streets, trying to keep them alive with nothing. This time, she did not have to do any of it alone.

A sweet, affectionate girl who settled right in Credit: Snuggle Fluff

From the start, Abby charmed everyone at the shelter. “She’s sweet and affectionate and a master biscuit maker,” her foster shared with LoveMeow, kneading away contentedly from the moment she checked in.

She came with a mother’s résumé, too. “I can already tell she’s gonna be an excellent mom,” her foster wrote while Abby was still expecting, and the prediction held up the instant the kittens arrived.

Five hungry newborns, one very capable mom Credit: Snuggle Fluff

Watching Abby with her newborns, it is clear she has done this before. She curls around the whole row of them, keeping every kitten fed and warm without a wasted motion.

The proof was in the details. The babies were already clean and dry before anyone found them that morning, the hardest part handled entirely on her own, in the dark.

Small enough to fit in a palm Credit: Snuggle Fluff

Those first days were all about eating and sleeping. The five kittens tucked against Abby’s side and nursed around the clock, growing by the hour while she kept them close.

For a mother who once had to find food and shelter for babies like these on the street, the quiet of a warm foster room was a world away from everything she had known.

Worn out from the hard work of being a newbornCredit: Snuggle Fluff

Between meals, the kittens did what newborns do best, sleeping in a heap with their paws tucked and their faces scrunched. Abby kept watch over every nap.

Her foster summed up the scene with two words. The litter was a bunch of “little piglets,” five of them, eating and dozing and growing rounder by the day.

The whole family, fed and contentCredit: Snuggle Fluff

Each of the five got a name. There are four grays and one brown tabby, which makes Honey easy to pick out as Mama Abby’s only brown kitten. Her sister Harley rounds out the two girls, and the boys are Happy, Halo, and Fred.

Abby manages all five at once like the seasoned mother she is, settling the whole pile in to nurse and keeping track of every last one.

Happy, getting a wash whether he holds still or not Credit: Snuggle Fluff

Happy earns his name, squirming and scooting around even as Abby tries to groom him. She stays patient, following the moving target with her tongue, determined to get him clean.

It is the kind of small, ordinary moment Abby never got to have in peace before. Here, she can fuss over a wiggly kitten without one eye on the street.

From newborns to proper little cats in a matter of weeksCredit: Snuggle Fluff

They did not stay tiny for long. The helpless newborns from those first photos filled out fast, trading the nursing pile for wobbly first steps around the room.

Every week brought something new, a little more weight, a little more coordination, a little more mischief. Abby watched it all unfold from the middle of the chaos.

Rarely more than a paw apartCredit: Snuggle Fluff

By three weeks, the kittens were walking, playing, and sprouting their first teeth. Now, at five weeks, they are a full-on pack, tumbling over each other and exploring every corner of the room.

They are healthy and thriving, hitting every milestone right on schedule. Their mother made sure of it.

Happy and HoneyCredit: Snuggle Fluff

Honey has found the toy basket. She bats a fuzzy green bug around the blanket with the fierce focus of a cat ten times her size, swatting it clear across the room and pouncing after it.

Each of the five is finding its own way now, discovering toys, blankets, and the endless entertainment of four siblings to climb on.

Change happens fast as a kittenCredit: Snuggle Fluff

The personalities are already showing. Fred is, in his foster’s words, “so chunky,” the solid one of the bunch, while Halo has a signature move. “Silly Halo always has his feet in the air,” her foster said of the kitten who cannot seem to nap any other way.

At five weeks old, the litter has a remarkable amount of character between them, and plenty of growing still to do.

Fred then and now Credit: Snuggle Fluff

Watching them grow has been the easy part, because Abby made the hard part look effortless. “She is so relaxed knowing her kittens are safe,” her foster said, a calm a street cat rarely gets to feel.

Not long ago, Abby was raising kittens on the streets with no one to help and no promise any of them would make it. Between feedings these days, she kneads her blanket like the master biscuit maker she is, perfectly at ease. This time she has had nothing to do but be their mother, and when the kittens are grown, she will be spayed and finally get to enjoy being a cat again.

5 weeks already!Credit: Snuggle Fluff

item.title: Somebody Named Five Feral Kittens After Squash Varieties, It Explains Something About Rescue Work
item.description:
Five feral kittens who could not be touched without thick gloves were named Acorn, Spaghetti, ButterNut, Patty Pan and Zucchini. A year of rescue stories later, the litter names are the detail that stays with us.

Norman, Stanley, Bernard, Eugene, and Otis HenryCredit: Lori White

Nobody makes rescues do this. Litters could be numbered, and many are at intake. But somewhere between the carrier and the foster room, somebody sits down and decides these five particular kittens will be squash varieties, and from that moment they stop being a litter and start being individuals.

LoveMeow reports original cat rescue stories every day, which means we read a great many of these naming decisions. On National Cat Day, here are the best of this year, and what they are actually for.

The food rule

Food wins. It is not close.

When Sonora Cat Rescue, an all-volunteer group in Sonora, California, brought in five six-week-old kittens from a feral colony this September, they arrived unhandleable. Two days later they were a different set of animals, and the rescue's president, Sadie Anderson, had already given them a collective nickname that stuck.

"It hasn't even been 2 full days, and these spice nuggets I couldn't grab without gloves are now approaching me, leaning into scritches, and even purring," she told LoveMeow.

Spice nuggets. Acorn, Spaghetti, ButterNut, Patty Pan and Zucchini. Anderson also explained why those two days mattered so much, which is the part most people do not know. "When kittens are 5 to 8 weeks old, their personalities are very malleable," she said. "Once they get to be around 9 weeks old, that window slams shut." Five kittens came out of a colony inside that window, and five kittens got to be squash.

Read the spice nuggets' full story

Squash kittensCredit: Sonora Cat Rescue

At Merced SPCA in Merced, California, a tortoiseshell stray came in with five kittens and became Momma Muffin. Her litter was the Breakfast Bunch: Waffles, Pancake, Omelet, Biscuit and Toast.

Read Momma Muffin's full story

Momma Muffin and her kittensCredit: Merced SPCA

And at the Orphan Kitten Project at UC Davis, two bonded siblings pulled out of an overcrowded shelter were named Mahi Mahi and Mackerel, which is the only fish-themed litter we came across all year and deserves recognition for it.

Read Mahi Mahi and Mackerel's full story

Mahi Mahi and MackerelCredit: Orphan Kitten Project at UC Davis

The cheese brothers of Sandy Springs

During a TNR effort in Sandy Springs, Georgia, volunteers with Catz4life kept running into the same light orange and white female. She had a particular talent: every litter she produced came out looking exactly like her. This round she had four boys, each one a near-perfect copy.

Somebody on that team has a sense of humor, because all four went out as cheeses. Ricky is short for Ricotta and Reggie for Reggiano. Their brothers went home as Colby Jack and Monterey Jack, better known as Colby and Monty.

Getting to them was not funny at all. "They were hiding way under the crawl space of a home, and our TNR team had to crawl under there to get them," Aimee with Catz4life told LoveMeow. Their mother turned out to be smarter than the traps, slipped through, raised one more identical litter, and was eventually caught, spayed and returned to her territory.

Colby and Monty were adopted quickly. Ricky and Reggie are still waiting.

Read Ricky and Reggie's full story

Ricky & ReggieCredit: catz4life

The chocolate family

Someone left a bird cage outside Abandoned Pet Rescue, a no-kill shelter in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. Inside it was a mother cat and four kittens, crowded into a space built for something with wings.

The shelter named her Godiva. Her kittens became Hershey, Twix, Kit Kat and M&M. Godiva was losing weight and the kittens were far too young to be alone, so a foster took the whole family home until the litter grew up and Godiva recovered.

Godiva was adopted. So were Hershey and M&M. Twix and Kit Kat are the two who were not, and they are still at the shelter, where Twix has developed a method for stopping people as they pass her room. "She'll stand up on her hind legs, leaning her back against the wall for balance," staff member Luna Carvajal told LoveMeow.

Read Twix and Kit Kat's full story

Twix and Kit KatCredit: Abandoned Pet Rescue

The litter named after horses, for a reason

Three kittens were found this July under piles of garbage in a dilapidated garage behind an abandoned house in the New Jersey suburbs, four weeks old, eyes crusted shut with infection. New York City Animal Rescue Girls took in the whole family, including their mother, whose milk had dried up.

Their foster named them Appaloosa, Palomino, and Caspian. Appaloosa is the calico and the only girl, Palomino the orange and white boy, Caspian is the tuxedo.

The theme was not arbitrary. She chose horse breeds in honor of the New York carriage horses that advocates have been working to retire to sanctuary. Three kittens out of a garbage pile in New Jersey are carrying a campaign about horses in Manhattan, and almost nobody who reads their names will ever know it.

That is the thing about a naming theme. It is usually a message from the person who did the hardest part, and it is usually addressed to nobody.

Read Appaloosa, Palomino, and Caspian's full story

Caspian, Palomino, AppaloosaCredit: NYCARG

The Golden Years Gang

In September, someone noticed movement under a fallen tree on the grounds of a senior living facility on the south side of Indianapolis. Underneath were seven kittens, two and a half to three weeks old, and a mother who had been outdoors for months.

Alliance for Responsible Pet Ownership moved fast. "We couldn't say no to helping them, so we quickly made some calls, and within 15 minutes my husband and daughter arrived with old towels, Churus, and carriers," foster Lori White told LoveMeow.

The kittens were named for the place that sheltered them. Norman, Stanley, Bernard, Eugene, and Otis Henry are the five boys. Dottie and Pearl Louise are the two girls. Somebody christened the litter the Golden Years Gang, and it stuck, and it is the best litter name we published all year, because it turns the circumstance of their rescue into something with dignity in it.

All seven kittens are now spoken for.

Read the Golden Years Gang's full story

Millie and her babiesCredit: Lori White

The ones named for the worst night of their lives

Then there is the other category, and it is the one that stays with us.

Late on a Friday night in Chattanooga, Tennessee, Holly, a volunteer with SCRATCH, Inc., went looking for a kitten crying somewhere near a large drainpipe. She and her husband closed off the top of the pipe so he could not run into traffic, worked their way around to the far end, and played kitten sounds on a phone in the pitch dark so he would answer back. A rock slide had come down on him. Her husband found the tip of a tail with a flashlight and lifted the rocks off one at a time.

They named him Rocky. For the rocks, and for what it took to get out from under them.

Read Rocky's full story

RockyCredit: SCRATCH, Inc.

In Las Vegas, a six-week-old kitten weighing under two pounds was pressed against a concrete barrier on the Decatur Boulevard exit ramp while traffic came through. A truck driver working nights pulled over, picked him up, and then went looking for someone who would know what to do with a kitten. A neighbor pointed him to Homeward Bound Cat Adoptions.

They named him Freeway.

Read Freeway's full story

FreewayCredit: Homeward Bound Cat Adoptions

There is something quietly defiant in this. A cat gets named for the single worst thing that ever happened to him, and then he spends the next fifteen years being called it affectionately by people who feed him. The disaster becomes a nickname. Rocky doubled his weight in two weeks and now cannot sit still. A resident cat named Charles is teaching Freeway how to be a house cat.

What the naming is for

Rescue work is mostly logistics. Traps, transport, medication schedules, foster placements, phone calls at eleven at night. The naming is the one part of it that is purely optional, which is exactly why it is worth noticing.

A theme takes effort. Somebody has to look at five frightened animals that arrived as an emergency and decide they are squash varieties, or cheeses, or a gang of retirees. It is the first thing anyone does for them that is not medically necessary, and it is the moment a litter stops being a quantity.

Happy National Cat Day to everyone who has ever sat in a foster room at midnight trying to think of a fourth cheese.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do animal rescues give litters themed names?


Themed naming makes a litter easier to keep track of in records and in foster communication, but rescues and fosters describe it as something more than administrative. Naming a litter by theme is often the first non-medical thing done for kittens who arrived as an emergency, and it marks the point at which they are treated as individuals rather than as a group. Themes also make litters more memorable to potential adopters.

Who names rescue kittens?


Usually, it's the foster or the volunteer who brought them in. In the stories above, the themes came from a rescue president, a TNR team, a foster parent, and shelter staff. Occasionally, the name commemorates the rescue itself, as with Rocky, named for the rocks he was buried under, and Freeway, named for where a truck driver found him.

Can you adopt a whole litter together?


Sometimes, some bonded pairs are only placed together. Ricky and Reggie of the cheese brothers are being adopted as a pair, and Twix and Kit Kat remain at Abandoned Pet Rescue in Fort Lauderdale. Contact the organization named in each story for current availability.

Where can I read daily cat rescue stories?


LoveMeow publishes original cat rescue stories every day at lovemeow.com, sourced directly from rescue organizations, shelters, and foster families in the United States and internationally.

item.title: Cat Left in Taped-Up Box Behind a Garbage Can Greets Everyone With a Head Bump and Her Elegant Gray Mustache
item.description:
A white-and-gray cat was found taped inside a plain cardboard box behind a garbage can almost a year ago, and she has spent every morning since greeting whoever walks in with a head bump and the most elegant little gray mustache.

LadyCredit: AMA Animal Rescue

Lady’s story began on a chilly October morning last year. In the early hours before dawn, an AMA Animal Rescue team spotted her tucked inside a plain cardboard box, taped shut and shoved behind the street garbage cans.

There’s no telling how long she’d been there, possibly overnight, alone and confused in the dark. For such a rough way to be found, Lady took it with remarkable grace, calm and loving even then, just bewildered about how she had ended up there.

The team got her to safety and straight to their vets, who were relieved to find the three-year-old in good health. The hard part, it turned out, was still ahead of her.

First to say hello, every single morningCredit: AMA Animal Rescue

From her very first day, Lady’s personality shone through, and a year in a kennel hasn’t muted it. “She’s the first to greet you in the morning when you walk in the cat room,” AMA Animal Rescue shared with LoveMeow.

Her greeting of choice is a head bump. Walk into the cat room, and Lady is right there to say hello with a gentle bump of her head. The same warm welcome every morning, no matter how many mornings have gone by.

layful when she wants to be, with firm opinionsCredit: AMA Animal Rescue

Lady is both playful and relaxed. She’ll bat a good string toy around happily enough, but she has made her real preference clear.

“Lounging with her humans is her specialty,” the rescue shared. Given the choice, she would gladly spend a whole afternoon curled up at your side over any toy on the floor.

The lounging specialist, demonstratingCredit: AMA Animal Rescue

She means it, too. Lady is incredible at being relaxed. On the floor, next to you, or when her pink paws give you that afternoon wave, she is a cat who has clearly made relaxing into an art form.

Not much rattles her. After her start, she's settled into an easy, unbothered calm that makes her a soothing presence to sit with.

The distinguished gray mustache, in full viewCredit: AMA Animal Rescue

Then there’s the mustache. This nine-pound girl comes with a dapper gray smudge above her lip, “a very distinguished little gray mustache,” as the rescue puts it.

It gives her a permanently dignified look, like a cat who ought to have a tiny monocle to match. Paired with her steady yellow eyes, it makes her look as though she is quietly sizing up the room.

So many great posesCredit: AMA Animal Rescue

That is the bittersweet part of Lady’s story. Nearly a year has now gone by since she was found, and in all that time, she has not received a single adoption application.

Through every quiet day, she has kept her warmth. Her caregivers have been her steady company, keeping her healthy and loved, and Lady has repaid them by staying the same gentle, friendly girl she was on day one.

MultitaskingCredit: AMA Animal Rescue

These days, in the rescue’s words, Lady is “ready to leave her single-girl era behind.”

Around the other cats at the rescue, she is easy company, never aggressive and content to share the room. Her caregivers have watched her take the other residents entirely in stride, settling in among them with the same calm she brings to everything.

ady, the same sweet girl she has always beenCredit: AMA Animal Rescue

A year ago, Lady was found taped inside a box behind the garbage, calm, confused, and entirely alone.

Today she is in Brooklyn, healthy and affectionate still greeting every morning with a head bump, exactly the sweet girl she has been all along.

Share this story with your friends. View more on Lady and AMA Animal Rescue on Instagram @amaanimalrescue and Facebook, or by visiting amaanimalrescue.org.

item.title: Fragile Kitten Found in a Field Too Shut Down to Eat Has Decided to Become a Fluffy Gentleman in a Bow Tie
item.description:
A one-pound grey tabby kitten was found out in a field and didn't know how to eat. Now a one-year-old cat, he's grown into a fluffy gentleman wearing a tuxedo tie.

ConradCredit: Welcome To The Zoo

Look at Conrad today, and you’d never guess where he started. He’s a big, handsome, impossibly fluffy gray cat who turned one this year, the kind who commands a room just by sitting in it.

A year ago, the picture could not have been more different. Conrad was found alone in a field, a tiny kitten who was lethargic, dehydrated, and shutting down.

He landed at a local shelter that could not give him the round-the-clock care he needed, and a hard cutoff was already closing in. Conrad was running out of time, fast.

Barely a pound, and nearly out of timeCredit: Welcome To The Zoo

A community plea went out for Conrad with a hard deadline of 4 PM. If no one stepped up by then, this one-pound kitten was going to run out of chances.

A rescue stepped in and pulled him from the shelter just in time. He was stable enough to leave the shelter, but he wasn’t out of the woods yet, because this fragile baby still needed far more help than he could manage on his own.

Round-the-clock feedingsCredit: Welcome To The Zoo

Once he was stable, Conrad went into foster care with Welcome to the Zoo, a Tampa, Florida foster team, and the round-the-clock work began in earnest. Shut down and overwhelmed, he could not manage food on his own, so his foster fed him around the clock by syringe for the first few days.

Meal by meal, the tiny kitten got the hang of it. After days of patient hand-feeding, Conrad finally started eating on his own, the first real sign he was going to make it.

item.title: Cat Who Trusted No One When She Arrived at a Sanctuary Now Chats Away and Claims Every Corner Like She Owns It
item.description:
A dilute tortoiseshell cat trusted no one when she arrived at her new home, a Santuary. Now she chirps, chats, and claims every corner as if she owns it.

SageCredit: Milo’s Sanctuary

Sage’s start was a hard one. As a kitten, she was found on the side of a road, likely hit by a car, and ended up at a veterinarian’s office that planned to euthanize her. At first, a rescuer stepped in and refused to let that happen.

That rescuer raised her and loved her, but when hard times made it impossible to keep going, she made the difficult choice to surrender Sage to Milo’s Sanctuary in California so that she would be cared for. Choosing what was best for Sage over keeping her was its own hard act of love.

Sage is paralyzed in her back legs and needs diapers, special food, and supplements to stay clean and comfortable, all of it part of her daily routine now. What she needed most, though, was time, and a reason to trust again.

On the way to her new life, with a steadying hand nearbyCredit: Milo’s Sanctuary

The journey to the sanctuary was the start of everything that came next. Tucked into a carrier for the car ride with a gentle hand on her head, Sage watched the world go by on the way to a place she did not yet know was going to be home.

She had every reason to be guarded. She didn't know these people yet, and trust was not something she handed out, so she arrived braced for whatever came next.

Settling in among the sanctuary catsCredit: Milo’s Sanctuary

Settling into sanctuary life is a big adjustment for a cat who once had a home of her own, and Sage’s progress has come in a long run of small victories over her first couple of months. One by one, she has won them.

She has formed real bonds, first with sanctuary manager Mirissa, then with several resident cats, including a black-and-white tuxedo she can often be found alongside. She has also worked out exactly which corners of the sanctuary feel most like hers, and she scurries to them like she owns the place.

On the move, diaper and all Credit: Milo’s Sanctuary

Paralysis does not keep Sage in one place. She scoots herself from room to room, diaper and all, going wherever she has decided she wants to be and letting nothing slow her down.

Getting around on her own terms is its own kind of victory for a cat who arrived unsure of everything. These days she travels the sanctuary like a resident determined to explore every inch.

Curled up in a favorite spotCredit: Milo’s Sanctuary

When she has toured the place to her satisfaction, Sage curls into one of her chosen beds and sleeps without a worry in the world. The floral diaper is just part of the picture, as ordinary to her day as a collar.

Rest comes easily to her now, which says more about how safe she feels than almost anything else could. It is a long way from the cat who first arrived braced for the worst.

Lots to sayCredit: Milo’s Sanctuary

The biggest change of all is that Sage found her voice. “She’s learned her voice here as well,” Mirissa, the sanctuary manager, shared with LoveMeow. “When she doesn’t want something, she lets us and the other cats know.”

She is not shy about it, either. A cat who once kept everyone at a distance now has firm opinions and shares them freely, informing people and fellow felines alike exactly when she has had enough.

A happy chirp for a good scratch Credit: Milo’s Sanctuary

Not all of Sage’s talking is complaints. Pet her the way she likes, and she chirps, a small happy sound from a cat who has decided she rather enjoys the attention after all.

It is the same voice she once used to warn people off, now turned to telling them she is content. For a cat who started too guarded to be touched, a chirp under a stranger’s hand is no small thing.

Mealtime is taken very seriouslyCredit: Milo’s Sanctuary

Sage has grown comfortable enough to let anyone care for her now, down to the parts she once refused when she first arrived. She lines up at her raised bowl, licks her lips, and lets whoever is on duty help her through her day.

Her clearest welcome, though, is the catnip toy. Mirissa reports that Sage will happily share her favorite one with a visitor, nudging it toward whoever has come to see her. For a cat who used to want nothing to do with anyone, offering up her favorite thing is about the warmest invitation she has to give.

Fully at homeCredit: Milo’s Sanctuary

“The Sage who first arrived isn’t the same Sage now, and we mean that in such a good way,” Mirissa shared. “She was a bit hissy, a little distrusting, but she’s learned she’s safe with us.” Flopped belly-up in a cozy bed without a trace of that old wariness, she looks every bit the proof of it.

Sage arrived at Milo’s Sanctuary hissing and bracing for the next bad thing. Today she scoots through every room as if she owns it, chirps when someone scratches her the right way, and sleeps belly-up without a worry left in the world.

Share this story with your friends. View more on Sage and Milo’s Sanctuary on Instagram @milo_santuary and Facebook, with thanks to sanctuary manager Mirissa for her care. View Sage's dedicated page at milossanctuary.org.

item.title: Senior Cat Waited Through Multiple Pleas for Help, Now Cured, Her Raspy Meow Comes With Intense Snuggles
item.description:
A sweet senior cat waited through multiple community pleas for help. A rescue finally said yes, and that seventh chance gave her something extraordinary: a complete cure and her whole life back. Now she walks with a raspy meow and comes in close for snuggles.

MarianCredit: Shelby, Liberation Cat House

Marian’s road to this moment was not an easy one. She came to Liberation Cat House from their friends at Orange County Animal Services, in Orlando, FL, as an owner surrender, after being adopted from the shelter back in November.

Sadly, her medical needs turned out to be more than her owner could manage, and she found herself back in need of help. The shelter sent out six separate pleas for rescue on her behalf, hoping someone would step forward for this deserving senior girl.

All six went unanswered. Then, just when it mattered most, a spot opened up, and Liberation Cat House pulled her into their care.

A fresh start, at about ten years oldCredit: Shelby, Liberation Cat House

At around ten years old, Marian had been diagnosed with a thyroid condition, and her new rescue was determined to do right by her. They set their hopes on a remarkable treatment called I-131 radioiodine therapy, a single, painless injection that does not just manage the condition but can cure it outright.

After bloodwork and a referral to a specialized feline thyroid clinic, this brave senior girl was given her shot at a healthier life. For a cat who had been turned down again and again, it was the chance no one else had offered her.

See Marian in her playful element Credit: Shelby, Liberation Cat House

Watch her now, and you would never guess what she had been through. Marian plays with the easy enthusiasm of a much younger cat, batting and pouncing like a girl with energy to spare.

It is the clearest sign of how far she has come. Whatever her age on paper, Marian is bright, curious, and fully herself again.

Resting at the clinic that changed everythingCredit: Shelby, Liberation Cat House

The results could not have been more wonderful. Just before her treatment at the end of August, Marian’s thyroid levels were dangerously high.

Thirty days after her short stay at the NuCat Feline Hyperthyroid Clinic, those numbers had dropped all the way back into the healthy range. Marian was officially, completely cured.

Healing inside and out, with her coat filling back inCredit: Shelby, Liberation Cat House

Her triumph was made possible by her rescuers and a community of supporters who came together to help make her treatment happen. “It’s amazing what science can do,” Shelby, director and social media coordinator for Liberation Cat House, shared with LoveMeow.

Her fur is growing back in beautifully as she settles into the comfort and security of foster care. Every day, a little more of the healthy, beautiful cat underneath comes back into view.

She has a great deal to sayCredit: Shelby, Liberation Cat House

Now that she is healthy and thriving, Marian is ready to show the world what a delightful companion she is. She is wonderfully chatty, and has the very best purr motor, one that rumbles to life the moment she is happy.

She also has the most endearing raspy little voice. “She has this raspy meow that sounds more like it ought to belong to a haggard old tom cat,” Shelby shared with LoveMeow, and once Marian starts talking, it is hard not to answer her back.

A cat who lives for a good scratch Credit: Shelby, Liberation Cat House

Marian loves getting scratched around her ears, and everyone who meets her comments on how sweet she is. Offer her a hand and she leans in, purring, as though she has been waiting her whole life for exactly this.

She is a champion snuggler, too. “She loves to snuggle,” Shelby shared, and Marian has been known to try sharing a collarbone with her foster mom for the coziest cuddles imaginable, the kind of cat who wants to be as close as she can get.

Mid-sentence, as usualCredit: Shelby, Liberation Cat House

Marian also has many thoughts on other cats, and she is not shy about sharing them. She is not aggressive, exactly, just a senior lady who never quite learned the social graces and sees no earthly reason to start now. She will stride right up to another cat to investigate, personal space being entirely optional, with the breezy confidence of a girl who has decided the rules are more of a loose suggestion.

It is all part of the package with this senior girl: opinionated, affectionate, and endlessly interested in everything happening around her. She has clearly decided she has a lot of living left to do, and manners can catch up later.

Sunlit and contentCredit: Shelby, Liberation Cat House

Every bit of Marian’s remarkable turnaround is thanks to the people who stepped forward when so many others could not.

From the shelter that kept pleading for her, to Liberation Cat House, which pulled her just in time, to the veterinary team who cured her, Marian finally found the champions she needed.

Marian, cured and content at lastCredit: Shelby, Liberation Cat House

Not long ago, Marian was a sick senior cat no one answered for, six times over. Today she is cured, comfortable, and chattering away in a foster home that adores her.

For a girl who waited so long for her yes, Marian is spending every day since exactly as she should, warm, healthy, and purring.

Share this story with your friends. View more on Marian and Liberation Cat House on Instagram @liberationcathouse and Facebook. Follow along with Shelby on Instagram @grimalkin_den.

item.title: Tiny Kitten Left Outside Kept Pawing at a Glass Door, and the Day It Opened, He Finally Got to Be a Baby
item.description:
A tiny kitten was left outside and left to face a world far too big for someone so small, and he spent his first frightening days pawing at a glass door. Once it was opened, he finally got to be the baby kitten he deserved to be.

JitsuCredit: Paws of Hope NYC

Jitsu’s beginning was a frightening one. This baby kitten was left outside, abandoned with no one to protect him and no understanding of the many dangers around him.

Imagine being so small in a world so big, with no idea where to turn for safety. At an age when he should have been chasing toys and napping in a warm lap, Jitsu was instead trying to work out how to survive.

The outside world makes no promises to a kitten like him.

Jitsu the day he was found Credit: Paws of Hope NYC

The footage of the day he was found is hard to forget. A tiny gray kitten sits alone at a glass door, reaching one small white paw up against it, as if he already understood that safety was on the other side and he needed someone to open it.

“This baby should be chasing toys, not searching for safety,” Gissell of Paws of Hope NYC shared with LoveMeow. He was far too little to be out there on his own, and he knew it.

Safe indoors, and finding his feetCredit: Paws of Hope NYC

Thankfully, someone stepped forward for Jitsu. One caring foster saw him and knew she couldn't leave him to fend for himself.

“Sometimes the only thing separating a rescue story from a tragedy is whether someone stepped forward in time,” Gissell shared with LoveMeow. She made a promise to give Jitsu the one thing the streets never could: a real chance, and she committed to it with her whole heart.

A kitten who finally feels safe enough to relaxCredit: Paws of Hope NYC

With that one decision, everything changed. Jitsu went from a tiny kitten with an uncertain future to a little one wrapped in safety and care, free at last to be a kitten.

In the comfort of his foster home, he could rest easy, protected and doted on for the first time in his life. The frightening days outside began to fade.

Toys, at last, instead of sidewalks Credit: Paws of Hope NYC

Safe indoors, Jitsu finally got to do the things a kitten his age is meant to do. There are toys to bat across the floor now, soft blankets to flop on, and people who come running when he calls.

“Jitsu deserved that opportunity to experience a better life, and I committed to giving it to him,” Gissell shared. He has taken that chance and run with it, growing brighter and bolder by the day.

Every outfit suits him, hat includedCredit: Paws of Hope NYC

These days Jitsu is a kitten with a personality as big as the world that once frightened him. His foster has discovered he is endlessly patient about being dressed up, and she takes full advantage, so he turns up in a bandana one day and a tiny cowboy hat the next.

He wears all of it like he was born for the camera, tolerating each new costume with the calm of a cat who knows he looks good. For a baby who started with nothing, he has grown into a little character who seems delighted by everything around him.

A feather toy and a very serious hunterCredit: Paws of Hope NYC

Under his foster’s devoted care, Jitsu has been given everything he needs to thrive. He is now neutered, fully vetted, and completely ready for the next chapter of his life.

The uncertain days of being alone outside are firmly behind him, replaced by the warmth and security every kitten deserves. He hunts his feather toy now with the focus of a cat twice his size, pouncing and tumbling until it finally surrenders.

item.title: Cat Abandoned at Park Inside a Carrier With Her Newborns Went On to Mother Two Litters, Nine Kittens in All
item.description:
A mama cat was found zipped inside a carrier and left in an Atlanta park with her five newborn kittens still beside her. Rather than let that cruelty define her, she raised that litter to adoption and then took in a second litter of orphans too, nine kittens in all.

Mama JagaCredit: Catz 4 Life, Inc.

Someone zipped Jaga into a pet carrier, carried her to a park, and walked away, leaving a mother cat and her tiny kittens sealed inside and set down in the grass. It is the kind of thing that is hard to understand.

She was found across from Park Grounds, in front of a yellow house, her babies still tucked in beside her. A Good Samaritan spotted the abandoned carrier and reached out for help, and that call is the reason this story has the ending it does.

Catz 4 Life was already full. They said yes anyway. “Our rescue is full, but we couldn’t let this little family go without a safe place,” Aimee of Catz 4 Life shared with LoveMeow.

The carrier Jaga and her kittens were found zipped inside, left in the parkCredit: Catz 4 Life, Inc.

Several people jumped into action to get the little family to safety, and the clinic at The Cat Doctor Atlanta took them in overnight. By the next day, Jaga and her kittens were safe, and the danger was behind them for good.

Jaga looked, understandably, a little bewildered by it all. “Mom looks understandably bewildered; what a terrible experience, but she is in a home full of lovely people, and we will make sure she never faces that kind of ordeal again,” Aimee told LoveMeow.

Safe at last, and finally able to restCredit: Catz 4 Life, Inc.

Settled into foster care, Jaga did exactly what she had been trying to do all along. She raised the five kittens who were abandoned alongside her, a tight little crew the rescue nicknamed the Thundercats, strong names for a litter of small fighters.

She was a natural at it, patient and steady, nursing, grooming, and watching over them as they grew from frightened babies in that carrier into bold, healthy kittens. One by one, all five of the Thundercats found homes of their own.

The Thundercats, the litter found in the carrier with JagaCredit: Catz 4 Life, Inc.

Most mothers would have called that a job well done. Jaga was not finished. When a separate litter of four orphaned kittens needed someone, she stepped up again, taking in a second crew the rescue called the Guardians of the Galaxy.

These babies weren't hers, and no one would have blamed her for turning away. A cat who had been through what she had could have been forgiven for keeping to herself.

The Guardians of the Galaxy kittens with their surrogate mother Jaga Credit: Catz 4 Life, Inc.

Instead, Jaga opened up and made room. She let the four orphans nurse and curl up against her, grooming them and settling them the same way she had her own, until her foster room was a cheerful scramble of kittens climbing over every surface and piling against her side.

She mothered the Guardians as though they had been hers from the start, and one by one, all four of them were adopted too. “She did her time raising nine kittens,” Aimee shared, her own five and four more she chose to love, and every one of those babies went on to a home of their own.

A chin scratch for a very deserving momCredit: Catz 4 Life, Inc.

It is a staggering amount of giving from a cat who had every reason to trust no one. Whatever happened to her in that park, Jaga answered it with more love than most cats have in them.

Now, for the first time in a long time, she has nobody to raise but herself. She has transitioned beautifully into her foster home, settling in with the other cats and easing into a quieter life with no kittens underfoot.

Enjoying the high life, child-free at lastCredit: Catz 4 Life, Inc.

She is, the rescue reported to LoveMeow, thoroughly enjoying her new child-free status. After everything she poured into those nine babies, she has earned every lazy afternoon of it.

And what a cat she is underneath all that devotion. Jaga is long, lean, and striking, with a sleek build the rescue suspects may carry a little Oriental Shorthair somewhere in her family tree.

Curled up and content, exactly as she should beCredit: Catz 4 Life, Inc.

She is as easygoing as she is elegant. “She’s a pretty chill cat,” Aimee shared, the kind of calm, affectionate companion who has clearly made her peace with the world despite being given every reason not to.

Every chapter of her turnaround was made possible by people who refused to look away, from the Good Samaritan who found the carrier, to the team at The Cat Doctor Atlanta who took the family in overnight, to the foster home that opened its doors.

Nine kittens, raised by one remarkable motherCredit: Catz 4 Life, Inc.

All nine of her kittens are grown and adopted now, scattered into homes that will never know how close they came to a very different start. Their mother made sure of that.

What is left is Jaga herself, the one member of this whole rescued family whose next chapter has not yet begun.

Jaga, relaxed Credit: Catz 4 Life, Inc.

The cat who was abandoned in a carrier still found it in herself to mother nine kittens, her own and others’, and to come through all of it gentle, elegant, and unbroken.

She has done her share of the caretaking, and then some. After everything Jaga gave, a lap of her own feels like the very least the world owes her.

item.title: Two Cats Left Together on Rescue Doorstep, Big Brother Makes Sure You Never Pet Just One
item.description:
Two tabby and white cats are two devoted brothers who were abandoned together on a rescue doorstep,

Stinker and PeanutCredit: Abandoned Pet Rescue

The brothers arrived most suddenly, left on the doorstep of Abandoned Pet Rescue one day last year. It was an uncertain beginning for the bonded pair, but they had landed with people ready to give them everything they needed, including the one thing that mattered most: the chance to stay together.

From the moment they came into care, it was clear Stinker and Peanut were a devoted duo. They are both big boys with big hearts, and they absolutely love to be doted on.

Their rescuers have delighted in getting to know each of them, because there is plenty to love about both.

Rarely more than a whisker apartCredit: Abandoned Pet Rescue

Stinker is the bigger of the two, a sweet and affectionate fellow who adores nothing more than attention from his favorite people, and he is especially fond of a good chin and back scratch.

Even when the attention is going to someone else, he finds a way in. “If you’re giving his brother, Peanut, some love, Stinker will mosey on over and gently nudge your hand, as if to say, ‘Don’t forget me!’” Abandoned Pet Rescue shared with LoveMeow.

Stinker, a big boy with an even bigger heartCredit: Abandoned Pet Rescue

“While he may be a little greedy when it comes to getting attention, it’s only because he has so much love to give,” the rescue shared.

And for all his wish to be the center of things, Stinker absolutely adores his brother. He can often be found grooming Peanut, patient and gentle, the bigger brother looking after the smaller one.

Stinker giving his brother a thorough washCredit: Abandoned Pet Rescue

The pure bliss on Peanut’s face whenever Stinker licks his cheek is too precious to miss. One brother grooms, the other melts, and the whole room goes quiet watching it.

It is the clearest picture of who these two are together. Whatever uncertainty they arrived with, they have always had each other.

See the brothers in one of their favorite moments Credit: Abandoned Pet Rescue

Watch them for even a minute, and the bond speaks for itself. Stinker settles in to groom, Peanut leans into every lick, and the two of them fold together into one content tangle of fur.

This is how they spend their quiet hours, side by side, looking after one another. It is a devotion that is a joy to witness, and it is the heart of their whole story.

PeanutCredit: Abandoned Pet Rescue

Peanut is a bit more shy and takes some time to warm up, but he is every bit as loving once he knows you. He asks for affection with the sweetest little nudges, and scratches on his head and chin are his absolute favorite.

With his pretty blue eyes and a little pink nose, this gentle boy is adorable, and his trust is well worth the wait. He needs only a patient hand, and he gives his whole heart in return.

Those eyes do a lot of the talkingCredit: Abandoned Pet Rescue

Peanut has also been diagnosed with diabetes, which means a special diet and insulin twice a day. It sounds daunting, but there is wonderful news that takes the worry out of it.

Peanut qualifies for Abandoned Pet Rescue’s Medical Adoption Program, which means all of his veterinary care will be provided through the rescue for the rest of his life. Beyond his twice-daily insulin and his special food, his days look like any other happy cat’s, and his future family can focus only on loving him.

The best naps are the ones taken togetherCredit: Abandoned Pet Rescue

The bond between them is the heart of everything. Stinker and Peanut are happiest when they are together, and they love nothing more than curling up in one huge, warm bundle of adorable kitty goodness.

They are a true pair, full of love and easy companionship. Where one of them settles, the other is never far behind.

Two big heartsCredit: Abandoned Pet Rescue

Every bit of the comfort they enjoy today is thanks to the dedicated team at Abandoned Pet Rescue, a no-kill shelter in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. They took in two abandoned boys and have cared for them with patience and devotion.

They have made sure this bonded pair stays together, because splitting up two brothers who have only ever had each other was never on the table.

When one finds a good spot, the other turns up tooCredit: Abandoned Pet Rescue

Their bond is not all quiet grooming and naps, either. When one of them finds a toy worth chasing or a warm patch of floor worth claiming, the other turns up a moment later, and the two of them end up tangled in the same game or stretched out in the same sunny corner.

Stinker and Peanut were left on a doorstep together last May, and they have been inseparable every day since. For two brothers who have only ever had each other, being apart was never going to be an option.

Best of budsCredit: Abandoned Pet Rescue
